title: When people are hostile towards us. Part 1
scripture_text: ‘’However, after his brothers had left for the festival, he went also, not publicly, but in secret. Now at the festival the Jewish leaders were watching for Jesus and asking, “Where is he?” Among the crowds there was widespread whispering about him. Some said, “He is a good man.” Others replied, “No, he deceives the people.” But no one would say anything publicly about him for fear of the leaders. Not until halfway through the festival did Jesus go up to the temple courts and begin to teach. The Jews there were amazed and asked, “How did this man get such learning without having been taught?” Jesus answered, “My teaching is not my own. It comes from the one who sent me. Anyone who chooses to do the will of God will find out whether my teaching comes from God or whether I speak on my own. Whoever speaks on their own does so to gain personal glory, but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is a man of truth; there is nothing false about him. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps the law. Why are you trying to kill me?” “You are demon-possessed,”the crowd answered. “Who is trying to kill you?” Jesus said to them, “I did one miracle, and you are all amazed. Yet, because Moses gave you circumcision (though actually it did not come from Moses, but from the patriarchs), you circumcise a boy on the Sabbath. Now if a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses may not be broken, why are you angry with me for healing a man’s whole body on the Sabbath? Stop judging by mere appearances, but instead judge correctly.”
devotional:
Do you ever notice how much hostility and anger is around these days?

Twenty years ago, the term ‘road rage’ was never used, but it has now become part of everyday life. In top-level football matches, no game is complete without extreme expressions of anger and hostility, normally directed at the referee, even when their decisions are proven to be correct. Or take a typical round of ‘Prime Minister’s Questions’ in the House of Commons in London, where the Government and Opposition trade hostilities and insults rather than actually debating the issues of the day.

On the roads, on the football pitch, in the workplace…sometimes at home; we live in a hostile world. Many of us know this to be true from personal experience. If you’ve ever had the misfortune of being hated by someone, or being on the receiving end of their hostility, you’ll know that there is probably nothing more lonely or terrifying.

Our English word ‘hostile’ is from the French word (same spelling) which means ‘of or belonging to an enemy’. It is a potent combination of cynicism, anger and aggression. In psychological terms, hostility has been described as the wilful refusal to accept evidence that one's perceptions of the world are wrong. It gives rise to the hostile person attempting to force or coerce others to come into line with their view, regardless how unlikely the outcome, regardless of the collateral damage.

Of course, ‘hostility’ isn’t just a 21st Century trait. It has marked humanity since the beginning of time. It was certainly around in Jesus’ day. It touched his life and made his relationship with others more difficult. Nowhere is this more evident than in chapter 7 of John’s account of Jesus life.

As we have already seen, Jesus is conscious of the fact that he is hated: “The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because because I testify that what it does is evil.” John 7:7. So, he is fully aware of what lies in wait for him in Jerusalem.

The question for us is how best to respond when someone has a hostile attitude towards us or if someone is aggressive and angry with us for no good reason? As we tag along with Jesus and join him in Jerusalem, we may discover some appropriate ways to manage hostile situations.

Setting the scene

Reading the early verses of John 7, we notice that the writer’s focus shifts from Jesus’ private life to the public domain, from familiarity to the unknown. Jesus’ journey takes him, and us, from a place of misunderstanding to an environment of animosity.

At Feast time it was normal for families to go together up to Jerusalem; usually whole villages would travel together. This ensured safety and added to the sense of celebration. However, John informs us that ‘After his brothers left for the festival, Jesus also went, though secretly, staying out of public view.’

The Greek word for ‘secret’ is kruptos meaning ‘hidden’ – it’s the word from which we get our English word ‘cryptic’.

I think this must have been a very lonely moment for Jesus. As his community, family and friends travel to Jerusalem with a sense of anticipation and joy, Jesus travels as a lone and solitary figure. He doesn’t want to draw attention to himself or put others at risk. Nor does he feel the need to prove himself or to rush into Jerusalem with blazing authority. He just quietly approaches the place of conflict, because he feels secure in his Father. But soon the secrecy of his arrival will be shattered.

To add to the tension, John informs us that at the Feast, ‘…the Jewish leaders were watching for Jesus and asking, “Where is he?” (NIV1984)

Even before he arrives into the city, Jesus has already been singled out for surveillance. The religious leaders are watching and waiting for the chance to pursue their murderous intent.

During the Feast of Tabernacles, Jerusalem would normally have been buzzing – with a sense of carnival and joy. But on this occasion, something felt different, something wasn’t right.

John tells us that:

‘’Among the crowds there was widespread whispering about him. Some said “He is a good man.” Others replied, “No, he deceives the people.” But no- one would say anything publicly about him for fear of the Jews. (v12)

This is very descriptive of the atmosphere in the city. Jesus is a marked man and both he and the crowds know it.

The Greek word for whispering is goggusmos. It means ‘sullen discontent, murmuring, criticism.’ It describes the low, threatening and discontented muttering of a mob that distrusts its leaders and is on the verge of an uprising. It is always associated with rebellion.

The Jewish leaders were expert at creating an atmosphere of fear, and the people of Jerusalem are being very careful about what they say concerning Jesus. It must have been a strange and difficult situation for Jesus to be in. The atmosphere is heavy with hostility and fear; people are glancing at Jesus as they whisper to each other.
prayer: Father thank you that Jesus understands when we are faced with tense and hostile situations.
